idiom_name: javax.money MonetaryAmount with the Moneta Money implementation
implementation_notes: On the JVM the pattern has a standard: JSR 354 defines MonetaryAmount, CurrencyUnit, MonetaryOperator and MonetaryRounding, and the Moneta reference implementation provides Money (BigDecimal-backed, immutable, thread-safe, final) alongside FastMoney. The classic hand-rolled class therefore collapses into javax.money plus a provider dependency, with java.math.BigDecimal and java.util.Currency remaining the primitives underneath for code that must stay dependency-free. Keep the hand-rolled route only where a JSR 354 provider is unacceptable, and then copy the API shape: immutable, currency-checked arithmetic, explicit rounding, equals on amount plus currency.
pitfalls: JSR 354 equality includes the implementation type, so Moneta Money and FastMoney with the same amount and currency are not equal and must not be mixed carelessly.
Moneta initialises Money with MathContext.DECIMAL64 (16 digits), so large totals need an explicit, wider MonetaryContext.
BigDecimal.divide throws ArithmeticException on a non-terminating quotient unless a MathContext or scale is supplied.
java.util.Currency knows the code but not the minor-unit exponent, so the scale must come from the rounding provider or the application.

variants.name: Moneta FastMoney (long-backed, fixed scale)
variants.implementation_notes: FastMoney is the latency-oriented sibling in the same reference implementation: a fixed-scale amount backed by a long instead of BigDecimal, giving roughly 19 digits and much cheaper arithmetic for order and trading style workloads. It implements the same MonetaryAmount contract, so it can be swapped for Money behind the interface, but its limited precision and its fixed scale make it the wrong choice for tax, interest and accrual maths.
pitfalls: Its precision is far below BigDecimal, so compounding totals drift where Money would not.
Money.from(FastMoney) widens but does not restore lost precision, and equals across the two types is false by design.

variants.name: Hand-rolled BigDecimal plus java.util.Currency
variants.idiom_name: final class Money { BigDecimal amount; java.util.Currency currency; }
variants.implementation_notes: The pre-JSR route, still everywhere in legacy code: a final immutable class holding BigDecimal and java.util.Currency, with plus/minus that throw on mismatch, multiply/divide restricted to scalars, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN applied through setScale, and an allocate(int n) that distributes the remainder. It is fully workable, but the currency table, the ISO exponent, the rounding object and the FX handling are all yours; adopt JSR 354 when a library may enter the stack, because the standard already encodes these decisions.
pitfalls: java.util.Currency carries no exponent, so the default fraction digits must be looked up elsewhere or hard-coded (and then rot).
BigDecimal.equals compares scale as well as value, so new BigDecimal("1.0") is not equal to new BigDecimal("1.00") unless compareTo is used.
Division without a MathContext throws, and unrounded divide-then-round sequences lose minor units.
